title: Load Balancers and Application Gateway
description: Understand when to use Azure Load Balancer versus Application Gateway, and how to configure backend pools and probes.

data.text: Azure offers two main services for distributing traffic: the Azure Load Balancer and the Azure Application Gateway. They solve different problems, and choosing the right one depends on whether you need simple network-level load balancing or more advanced application-level routing.

The Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 of the OSI model, the transport layer. It distributes inbound traffic across healthy virtual machines using a simple round-robin or five-tuple hash. It is ideal for basic high-availability scenarios like scaling out web servers or database replicas.

data.title: Load Balancer basics
items: Distributes traffic using a five-tuple hash
Supports inbound NAT rules for RDP or SSH
Works with availability sets and availability zones

data.text: The Application Gateway works at layer 7, the application layer. It can route traffic based on URL paths, host headers, and HTTP headers. This makes it perfect for hosting multiple websites behind one public IP, or routing API traffic to different backend pools based on the request URL.

data.title: Application Gateway basics
items: Routes traffic based on URL path, host name, or headers
Includes a Web Application Firewall option

cards.title: Azure Load Balancer
cards.description: Layer 4 load balancing for TCP and UDP traffic across VMs.

cards.title: Application Gateway
cards.description: Layer 7 load balancing with advanced routing and WAF capabilities.
cons: Higher latency than LB due to layer 7 processing

data.text: Both services use backend pools, which are collections of IP addresses, NICs, or VM scale sets that receive traffic. Probes are health checks that determine whether a backend instance is healthy enough to receive traffic. If a probe fails, the service stops sending traffic to that instance.

data.title: Create a Load Balancer with a backend pool and probe using Azure CLI
data.content: Azure CLI to create a Load Balancer with health probe and backend pool
data.code:
az network lb create \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --name MyLoadBalancer \
  --sku Standard \
  --frontend-ip-name Frontend \
  --backend-pool-name BackendPool

az network lb probe create \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --lb-name MyLoadBalancer \
  --name MyHealthProbe \
  --protocol tcp \
  --port 80

az network lb rule create \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --lb-name MyLoadBalancer \
  --name HTTPSRule \
  --protocol tcp \
  --frontend-port 443 \
  --backend-port 443 \
  --frontend-ip-name Frontend \
  --backend-pool-name BackendPool \
  --probe-name MyHealthProbe

data.text: Use the Load Balancer when you need fast, simple distribution of TCP or UDP traffic across identical VMs. Use the Application Gateway when you need to inspect HTTP requests, route traffic based on URL path, host name, or headers, or add a Web Application Firewall for protection against common web attacks.

data.title: Choose the Right Load Balancing Service
data.description: Read each scenario and decide whether a Load Balancer or Application Gateway is the better choice.
steps: Scenario 1: You have three identical database replicas on TCP port 1433.
Scenario 2: You host two web apps, app1.contoso.com and app2.contoso.com, on the same public IP.
Scenario 3: You need to inspect HTTP traffic for SQL injection patterns.
data.expectedOutcome: Scenario 1: Load Balancer, Scenario 2: Application Gateway, Scenario 3: Application Gateway with WAF.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Load Balancer is layer 4 and fast for TCP/UDP.
Application Gateway is layer 7 and supports HTTP routing and WAF.
Backend pools hold the receiving resources.
Probes determine if a backend instance is healthy.
data.takeaway: Pick the tool that matches the layer and features your workload actually needs.
